mainTopic: Agreement (דעת) when bringing another person's קרבן according to שמואל and עולא; a husband's protest (מודעא) against a forced גט; and how בית דין announces a sale of orphans' and הקדש property.
overview: The גמרא finishes a ברייתא that seems to contradict שמואל: someone else's עולה or שלמים counts even without the owner's agreement. שמואל answers that the ברייתא is talking about the time of offering (שעת כפרה), while he meant the time the animal is set aside (שעת הפרשה). עולא holds the reverse: an עולה needs no agreement at שעת הפרשה, but every קרבן needs agreement at שעת כפרה. A second ברייתא requires agreement for all קרבנות, and each אמורא places it at a different stage. רב פפא sums up: the ברייתות don't clash with each other or with either אמורא, but שמואל and עולא truly disagree. Next, רב ששת rules that a husband's advance protest (מודעא) against a גט stays in force even if he later agrees, unless he clearly cancels it, as the משנה's words 'until he says' show. The פרק האומר משקלי ends. A new פרק opens with a משנה: בית דין announces a sale of orphans' property for thirty days and הקדש property for sixty days, morning and evening. The גמרא explains this timing and what the announcer must say, including who will receive the money.

steps.title: The end of the ברייתא that seems to contradict שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes its two cases. For someone else's חטאת or אשם, it counts only with the owner's agreement. For someone else's עולה or שלמים, it counts with or without his agreement. This seems to go against שמואל, who said an עולה needs agreement.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he brought the other person's חטאת or אשם with his agreement, the owner has fulfilled his obligation. Without his agreement, he has not. If someone says, 'I take upon myself the עולה and שלמים of so-and-so,' the owner has fulfilled his obligation whether or not he agreed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא it started quoting earlier, and this ברייתא is being used as a challenge against שמואל. The second half, about עולה and שלמים, is what causes the problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא draws a line between two kinds of קרבנות. חטאת and אשם need the owner's agreement, but עולה and שלמים work even without it. Since שמואל said an עולה does need the owner's agreement, the ברייתא looks like it contradicts him.

keyTerms.meaning: With his knowledge and agreement (consent)
He has fulfilled his obligation
Burnt offering, burned completely on the מזבח
Peace offering
'So-and-so's is upon me': I take on the obligation of another person's קרבן

steps.confusionAlert: The first line here is not a new rule. It is the end of the ברייתא's first case, about another person's חטאת and אשם, which started before this section.

phrases.english: With his consent, he has fulfilled his obligation;
without his consent, he has not fulfilled his obligation.
"The burnt offering and peace offering of so-and-so are upon me,"

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין לְדַעַת בֵּין שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעַת — יָצָא.
phrases.english: whether with consent or without consent, he has fulfilled his obligation.

steps.triggerLanguage: עוֹלָתוֹ וּשְׁלָמָיו שֶׁל פְּלוֹנִי עָלַי בֵּין לְדַעַת בֵּין שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעַת יָצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted just before this section as a challenge to שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's statement that an עולה needs the owner's consent.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says another person's עולה counts even without the owner's consent. That seems to directly contradict שמואל.

steps.title: שמואל: the ברייתא is about the time of offering, and I was talking about the time of setting aside
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers that the ברייתא is talking about שעת כפרה, when the owner already agreed at the earlier stage of setting the animal aside. His own rule is about שעת הפרשה itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל can say to you: That ברייתא is talking about the time of atonement, since the owner already agreed at the time the animal was set aside. When I said consent is needed, I meant at the time the animal is set aside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for שמואל by splitting the קרבן process into two moments: setting the animal aside, and offering it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no real contradiction, because the ברייתא and שמואל are talking about different stages. At the offering stage, the owner's agreement is not needed again because he already agreed when the animal was set aside. שמואל's rule that an עולה needs consent applies only to the setting-aside stage.

keyTerms.meaning: The time of atonement: when the קרבן is actually offered
The time of setting aside: when an animal is designated as a קרבן
He agreed (was willing)

steps.whyThisMatters: This answer creates the two-stage framework (הפרשה and כפרה) that the rest of the discussion depends on.

phrases.english: Shmuel could say to you:
When that baraita was taught, it was about the time of atonement,
since he already consented at the time of setting aside;
when I said it, I meant at the time of setting aside.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ שְׁמוּאֵל כִּי תַּנְיָא הָהִיא בִּשְׁעַת כַּפָּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: different stages of the קרבן process (הפרשה and כפרה).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say an עולה never needs the owner's consent, which would contradict שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is talking about שעת כפרה, where consent was already given earlier. שמואל requires consent for an עולה at שעת הפרשה.

steps.title: שמואל disagrees with עולא, who holds the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that this view of שמואל disagrees with עולא. עולא says the only difference between חטאת and עולה is at שעת הפרשה: a חטאת needs consent then, and an עולה does not. At שעת כפרה, every קרבן needs consent.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with עולא, because עולא said: The only difference they made between a חטאת and an עולה is that a חטאת needs consent at the time of setting aside, and an עולה does not. But at the time of atonement, for both of them: with consent, he has fulfilled his obligation; without consent, he has not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that שמואל's answer puts him in disagreement with עולא, and then quotes עולא's full rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל and עולא are mirror images. שמואל says an עולה needs consent at הפרשה but not at כפרה. עולא says an עולה does not need consent at הפרשה, but every קרבן needs consent at כפרה. So עולא must read the ברייתא's 'with or without consent' for עולה as talking about the setting-aside stage.

keyTerms.meaning: It disagrees (with another opinion)
They did not distinguish (the only difference they made was...)
Sin offering
This one and that one: both alike

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל: an עולה needs consent at הפרשה, but at כפרה consent is not needed again. עולא: a חטאת needs consent at הפרשה and an עולה does not, but at כפרה all קרבנות need consent.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix them up. The two opinions are reversed: each one says consent matters for the עולה at the stage where the other says it doesn't.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Ulla,
phrases.notes: "This" is שמואל's answer from the last step.

phrases.english: for Ulla said:
They did not distinguish between a sin offering and a burnt offering

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא שֶׁחַטָּאת צְרִיכָה דַּעַת בִּשְׁעַת הַפְרָשָׁה,
phrases.english: except that a sin offering requires consent at the time of setting aside,

phrases.aramaic: וְעוֹלָה אֵין צְרִיכָה דַּעַת בִּשְׁעַת הַפְרָשָׁה,
phrases.english: and a burnt offering does not require consent at the time of setting aside;
but at the time of atonement, for both this and that:
with consent, he has fulfilled his obligation;
without consent, he has not fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that שמואל's answer puts him in disagreement with עולא, and presents עולא's opposite framework.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to עולא, a חטאת needs the owner's consent at הפרשה and an עולה does not. At כפרה, all קרבנות need the owner's consent.

steps.title: A ברייתא that requires agreement for every קרבן
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if a person takes on someone else's חטאת, אשם, עולה or שלמים, it counts only with the owner's agreement. This seems to challenge both שמואל and עולא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: If someone says, 'So-and-so's חטאת, אשם, עולה and שלמים are my responsibility,' then if he brings them with the owner's agreement, the owner has fulfilled his obligation. Without his agreement, he has not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that seems to clash with what שמואל and עולא just said. This ברייתא puts עולה and שלמים in the same group as חטאת and אשם: all of them need the owner's agreement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא said an עולה or שלמים counts even without the owner's agreement. This ברייתא says even an עולה needs agreement. So whichever stage we put this ברייתא at, it seems to clash with someone: עולא said an עולה needs no agreement at שעת הפרשה, and שמואל read the first ברייתא as saying no agreement is needed at שעת כפרה.

keyTerms.meaning: So-and-so; some other person
Upon me; 'I take it on myself' (the wording of a promise)
With the owner's knowledge and agreement
He has fulfilled his obligation

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this ברייתא up with the first one. The first ברייתא said עולה and שלמים count without agreement. This one says all four need agreement. That difference is the whole reason for the question.

phrases.english: They raised an objection: His sin offering and his guilt offering
his burnt offering and his peace offering of so-and-so are upon me,
with consent, he has fulfilled his obligation;
phrases.notes: 'Consent' means the agreement of the owner, the person who was obligated to bring the קרבן.

phrases.english: without consent, he has not fulfilled his obligation!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges both positions just laid out (שמואל in Step 2 and עולא in Step 3) with a new ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא requires agreement even for עולה and שלמים. That seems to clash with שמואל (no agreement needed for an עולה at שעת כפרה) and with עולא (no agreement needed for an עולה at שעת הפרשה).

steps.title: Each אמורא places the ברייתא at a different stage
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the ברייתא is about שעת הפרשה. עולא says it is about שעת כפרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל explains the ברייתא as talking about the time the animal is set aside. עולא explains it as talking about the time of atonement.
steps.whatsHappening: Each אמורא answers the question by placing the ברייתא at the stage where, by his own view, agreement is needed even for an עולה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, an עולה needs agreement at שעת הפרשה, so the ברייתא fits if it is talking about that stage. For עולא, every קרבן needs agreement at שעת כפרה, so the ברייתא fits if it is talking about that stage. The same ברייתא works for both of them, just at opposite stages.

keyTerms.meaning: He sets it up as; he explains the source as talking about a certain case
The time of setting the animal aside as a קרבן
The time of atonement, when the קרבן is actually offered

phrases.english: Shmuel establishes it as referring to the time of separating the animal;
Ulla establishes it as referring to the time of atonement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 4 for each אמורא separately.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Placing the source in a specific case (אוקימתא), with each אמורא choosing a different stage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא requiring agreement for an עולה clashes with both שמואל and עולא.
steps.terutzMaskana: For שמואל it is about שעת הפרשה; for עולא it is about שעת כפרה. Each one fits it into his own rule.

steps.title: רב פפא: the two ברייתות don't contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא sums up: one ברייתא is about שעת כפרה and the other is about שעת הפרשה, so they don't contradict each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The ברייתות don't contradict each other. This one is about the time of atonement, and that one is about the time of setting the animal aside.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא steps back and gives a summary of the whole discussion. First he shows that the two ברייתות can live together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One ברייתא says an עולה needs no agreement, and the other says it does. That looks like a contradiction, but it disappears once each ברייתא is placed at a different stage. רב פפא doesn't say yet which ברייתא goes with which stage, because that depends on whose view you follow.

keyTerms.meaning: The ברייתות (teachings from the time of the משנה)
With each other
They are not difficult; there is no contradiction
This one ... that one (each source in its own case)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
The baraitot do not contradict each other;
phrases.notes: He means the first ברייתא (from Step 1) and the new one from Step 4.

phrases.english: this one is at the time of atonement,
that one is at the time of separating the animal.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: מַתְנְיָיתָא אַהֲדָדֵי לָא קַשְׁיָין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the answers in Step 5, רב פפא gives an overall summary, starting with how the ברייתות fit together.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two ברייתות don't clash: one is about שעת כפרה and the other is about שעת הפרשה.

steps.title: Neither ברייתא contradicts the אמוראים, but they disagree with each other
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא continues: שמואל places the first ברייתא at שעת כפרה and the second at שעת הפרשה, and עולא does the reverse. So the ברייתות fit both אמוראים, but שמואל and עולא really do disagree.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתות also don't contradict the אמוראים. שמואל explains the first one as talking about the time of atonement and the last one as talking about the time of setting aside. עולא explains them the opposite way. The אמוראים certainly disagree with each other.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא finishes his summary. Each אמורא can fit both ברייתות into his own view, but the two אמוראים still argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, the first ברייתא (no agreement for an עולה) is about שעת כפרה, and the second (agreement needed) is about שעת הפרשה. עולא flips it: no agreement for an עולה at הפרשה, but agreement for everything at כפרה. So the sources don't decide between them, and their argument stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: The Amoraim (here, שמואל and עולא)
The first one (the first ברייתא)
The last one (the second ברייתא)
The reverse; the opposite way
They certainly disagree

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל: an עולה needs agreement at שעת הפרשה but not at שעת כפרה. עולא: an עולה needs no agreement at שעת הפרשה, but every קרבן needs agreement at שעת כפרה. Both ברייתות fit each of them.

phrases.english: For the amora'im too, it is not difficult:
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'and the אמוראים' (round brackets). The corrected wording in square brackets says 'for the אמוראים.'

phrases.english: Shmuel establishes the first one as the time of atonement,
and the last one as the time of separating the animal;
Ulla establishes them the reverse way.
The amora'im certainly disagree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב פפא's summary from Step 6, now matching the ברייתות to each אמורא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברייתות fit both שמואל and עולא, each placing them at opposite stages, so the argument between the אמוראים stays real.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב פפא needed to say all this, since it seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא's summary: we already saw all of this, so what does his summary add? This sets up the next step, which explains what he was teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 2, 3 and 5 already showed how each Amora handles each ברייתא. So repeating it seems pointless, and the גמרא wants to know what new point רב פפא is making.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (asking why a statement was needed at all)

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why רב פפא's summary in Steps 6 and 7 was needed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Everything in the summary was already clear from the earlier answers, so it seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The summary shows exactly what שמואל meant
steps.stepSummary: Without רב פפא, we might think שמואל meant agreement is needed even at שעת הפרשה (on top of שעת כפרה), even though the first ברייתא would then refute him. רב פפא teaches that שמואל requires agreement only at שעת הפרשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: What does שמואל mean by 'at the time of setting aside'? Even at the time of setting aside, and even though the first ברייתא is a refutation of him. So רב פפא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'obvious' question by showing a mistake we could have made about שמואל without רב פפא's summary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might have read שמואל as saying an עולה needs agreement 'even' at שעת הפרשה, which means also at שעת כפרה. If so, the first ברייתא (no agreement for an עולה) would refute him, and we might think he holds his view anyway. רב פפא's summary shows that שמואל places the first ברייתא at שעת כפרה, so he needs agreement only at שעת הפרשה and is not refuted.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (a mistaken idea the גמרא is about to correct)
Even; also
A refutation; a source that knocks down a view
It teaches us (the new point)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב פפא, שמואל needs the owner's agreement for an עולה only at שעת הפרשה, not at שעת כפרה, so neither ברייתא refutes him.

phrases.english: Lest you say:
What is 'at the time of separating' that Shmuel said?
Even at the time of separating,
phrases.notes: 'Even' means also at הפרשה, on top of כפרה, so agreement would be needed at both stages.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּהָךְ קַמַּיְיתָא תְּיוּבְתֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: and even though that first one is a refutation of him,
phrases.notes: The 'first one' is the first ברייתא, which said an עולה counts even without agreement.

phrases.english: he teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' question of Step 8 by showing what רב פפא's summary adds.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the need for the statement by naming a mistake it prevents (מהו דתימא / קא משמע לן)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל means agreement is needed even at שעת הפרשה (so also at שעת כפרה), and he keeps this view even though the first ברייתא refutes it.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל needs agreement only at שעת הפרשה. He places the first ברייתא at שעת כפרה, so it does not refute him.

steps.title: רב ששת: A protest against a גט is valid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about forcing a husband to give a גט. רב ששת rules that a husband's advance protest (מודעא) against the גט is a real protest.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And likewise with women's divorce documents, we pressure him, etc.' רב ששת said: If someone made a declaration ahead of time against a גט, his declaration counts as a declaration.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה about pressuring a husband to give a גט. רב ששת then gives a ruling about a husband who protested in advance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גט has to be given willingly. If the husband declares in front of witnesses beforehand, 'I am only doing this because I am being forced,' רב ששת says that declaration works. It undoes the גט he later gives.

keyTerms.meaning: Women's divorce documents
We pressure or force (בית דין pushes him to act)
An advance declaration that what one is about to do is not done willingly
A divorce document

phrases.english: And likewise with women's divorce documents, we pressure him, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes our משנה. It goes on: we pressure him until he says 'I want to.'

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
One who made a declaration (of protest) about a get —
his declaration is a valid declaration.
phrases.notes: In other words, the protest works and the גט is not valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: הַאי מַאן דְּמָסַר מוֹדָעָא אַגִּיטָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה, separate from the שמואל and עולא discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A husband's מודעא made before giving a גט is effective and cancels the גט.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב ששת needed to say this, since it seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב ששת: everyone knows a protest made ahead of time cancels what follows, so why teach it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גט must be given willingly, so a clear protest should obviously ruin it. The question pushes the גמרא to find a less obvious case where רב ששת's ruling teaches something new.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (a challenge asking why a statement was needed)

phrases.english: Isn't that obvious?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רב ששת's ruling in step 10 adds anything new.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that a מודעא against a גט is valid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since a גט must be given willingly, an advance protest naturally cancels it. The ruling seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: The case where he was forced and later agreed
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת's ruling is needed for a case where the husband was forced, protested, and later seemed to agree without taking back his protest. The protest still stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where they forced him and he then agreed. You might have said that by agreeing he cancelled his protest. So רב ששת teaches us that he did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by pointing to a trickier case where רב ששת's ruling teaches something real.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Picture this: the husband protested, then later said he was willing and gave the גט. We might think his agreement quietly erased the protest. רב ששת teaches that the protest still holds until he clearly cancels it.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a special case)
They forced him
He agreed, became willing
He has cancelled it
He teaches us (that this is not so)

steps.confusionAlert: Agreeing to give the גט is not the same as cancelling the מודעא. Unless he clearly cancels the protest, it stays in force.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where they forced him and he then agreed,
phrases.notes: He had already made the protest. Later he went along with giving the גט but never said the protest was cancelled.

phrases.english: you might have said:
he has cancelled it (the protest),
so he teaches us (that he did not).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 11 by narrowing רב ששת's ruling to a less obvious case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ruling to a specific case (לא צריכא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Once he agreed and gave the גט, his earlier protest is automatically cancelled.
steps.terutzMaskana: The protest stays in force unless he clearly cancels it, so the גט is cancelled.

steps.title: The wording of the משנה supports רב ששת
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says 'until he says,' not 'until he gives.' This shows the husband must actually cancel his protest in words.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if it were not so, the משנה should say 'until he gives.' What does 'until he says' mean? Until he cancels his protest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב ששת's ruling comes from the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If just giving the גט willingly were enough to erase the protest, the משנה would have said 'until he gives.' Instead it says 'until he says (I want to).' That means he has to say out loud that he cancels his protest.

keyTerms.meaning: For if so (if the other view were right)
Let it teach (the משנה should have said)
Until he says
Cancels

steps.whatToRemember: A forced husband's מודעא cancels the גט unless he clearly takes it back. That is why the משנה says 'until he says,' not 'until he gives.'
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the גמרא reading the exact words of a משנה closely to draw out a practical rule about when a גט is valid.

phrases.english: For if so, let it teach: 'until he gives'!
phrases.notes: 'If so' means: if just giving the גט were enough to cancel the protest.

phrases.english: What does 'until he says' mean?
Until he cancels his declaration.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the answer in step 12 by drawing it from the wording of the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's rule that the protest remains unless clearly cancelled
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's wording 'עד שיאמר רוצה אני' instead of 'עד שיתן'

steps.title: הדרן — Closing פרק האומר משקלי
steps.stepSummary: The closing line for פרק האומר משקלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, האומר משקלי.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the traditional closing line that marks the end of the פרק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הדרן is not part of the argument. It is a formula said when finishing a פרק, expressing the hope to come back and learn it again.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you (said when finishing a perek)
The name of this perek: 'One who says: my weight (I pledge)'
Chapter

phrases.english: We will return to you, Ha'omer Mishkali.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the perek after the last discussion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The perek האומר משקלי is complete.

steps.title: The new משנה: announcing a sale for thirty or sixty days
steps.stepSummary: The new פרק opens with a משנה. Orphans' property is announced for thirty days, הקדש property for sixty days, and the announcement is made morning and evening.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: When בית דין values and sells orphans' property, it announces the sale for thirty days. For הקדש property, it announces for sixty days. The announcements are made in the morning and in the evening.
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק begins with a short משנה about announcing a property sale by בית דין before it happens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When בית דין must sell property (for orphans or for הקדש), it first sets a value (שום) and then announces it publicly so buyers can come. The announcement lasts thirty days for orphans and sixty days for הקדש. It must be made twice a day, morning and evening.

keyTerms.meaning: The appraisal: the price בית דין sets for property before selling it
Orphans; here, children who inherited property from their father
Property that belongs to the בית המקדש
They announce publicly

phrases.english: MISHNA: The appraisal of orphans' property is announced for thirty days
and the appraisal of consecrated property for sixty days
And they announce it in the morning and in the evening.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new פרק right after the closing line in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Orphans' property: thirty days of announcement; הקדש property: sixty days; announced morning and evening.

steps.title: Why announce specifically morning and evening?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what is special about morning and evening as the times for the announcement.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Why does the announcement happen specifically in the morning and in the evening?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question about the משנה: why exactly those two times? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on the משנה. The גמרא just wants to know the reason behind the timing, since the משנה gave no reason.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? Why this and not something else?

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is different about the morning and the evening?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the timing in the משנה of step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the announcement is made specifically morning and evening.

steps.title: Those are the times workers go out and come back
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: morning and evening are when workers leave for the fields and return. A buyer can send workers to check the field in the morning and ask them about it in the evening.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: The announcements are when workers go out to the fields and when they come back. In the morning, someone who wants to buy tells the workers, 'Go check the field for me.' In the evening, when the workers come back, he hears the announcement again, remembers what he asked, and says, 'Let me go ask them.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב explains that the announcement is timed so that buyers can easily get the field inspected by workers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The morning announcement reaches a buyer just as the workers head out, so he can ask them to look at the field on the way. The evening announcement reminds him when they return, so he goes and asks what they saw. This helps get the best price for the orphans or הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: The time workers go out to the fields (morning)
The time workers come back into town (evening)
Check it out, inspect it

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that בית דין tries hard to get the highest price when selling property for people who cannot protect themselves, like orphans and הקדש.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
At the time when the workers go out
and at the time when the workers come back in.
At the time when the workers go out:
so that if there is someone who would like to buy,
he can say to the workers:
Go check out the field for me.
At the time when the workers come back in:
so that he will remember that he told them,
and will say: Let me go and ask them.
phrases.notes: He means: let me ask the workers what they thought of the field.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב בִּשְׁעַת הוֹצָאַת פּוֹעֲלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Morning and evening are when workers leave and return, letting buyers have the field inspected and then ask about it.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב's explanation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that repeats the משנה's rule and adds the same explanation: workers going out and coming in.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches the same thing: Orphans' property is announced for thirty days, הקדש property for sixty days, and the announcement is morning and evening, when workers go out and when workers come back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that a ברייתא says exactly what רב said, which supports his explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא repeats the משנה word for word, but then adds the phrase about workers going out and coming in. That added phrase is the proof that רב's reason is correct.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא also teaches this, as support for what was just said
A teaching of the תנאים that was not included in the משנה

phrases.english: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא:
The appraisal of orphans' property is for thirty days,
and the appraisal of consecrated property is for sixty days,
and they announce in the morning and in the evening,
at the time when the workers go out
phrases.notes: This phrase is the part that matches רב's explanation.

phrases.english: and at the time when the workers come back in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב's answer in step 17 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב's explanation that the timing matches the workers' schedule.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that explicitly mentions the times workers go out and come in.

steps.title: The exact words of the announcement
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues and lists what the announcer says: which field, its borders, its quality, its price, an invitation to buy, and that the money goes to a wife's כתובה or a creditor's debt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The announcer says: 'The field of so-and-so, with these markers and these borders, is this good, and its value is this much. Anyone who wants to buy, come and buy. It is being sold to pay a wife her כתובה and a creditor his debt.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going and gives the actual words the announcer must say. This last line sets up the גמרא's next question about why the purpose of the sale must be mentioned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The announcement must describe the field clearly (whose it is, its borders, how good it is, and its price) so buyers know exactly what is offered. It also says why the field is being sold: to pay a widow's כתובה or a creditor's debt from the dead father's estate.

keyTerms.meaning: Its identifying signs, how you recognize the field
Its borders
The money a wife receives when the marriage ends
A creditor, someone who is owed money

steps.whatToRemember: בית דין announces orphans' property for thirty days and הקדש property for sixty days, morning and evening when workers come and go, describing the field clearly and saying why it is being sold.

phrases.english: The announcer says: The field of so-and-so,
with its markers and its borders,

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ הִיא יָפָה, וְכָךְ הִיא שׁוּמָא,
phrases.english: this is how good it is, and this is its appraised value,
anyone who wants to buy, let him come and buy,
in order to give the money to a wife for her marriage contract,
and to a creditor for his debt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא from step 18, adding the wording of the announcement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The announcer identifies the field, its borders, quality and value, invites buyers, and states that the proceeds go to a wife's כתובה or a creditor's debt.

steps.title: Why mention who gets the money?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the announcer must say the money is going to a wife's כתובה or a creditor's debt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need the announcer to say "in order to give a woman her כתובה and a creditor his debt"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the last item in the announcer's list from the ברייתא. It wants to know why a buyer would care who receives the money, and this sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other details (borders, quality, price) clearly help a buyer decide. But who gets paid seems to make no difference to the buyer, so the גמרא asks what this detail adds.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (a question about why a detail is included)
Her כתובה, the money a wife is owed from her husband's estate

phrases.english: Why do I need to say
"in order to give a woman her כתובה
phrases.notes: This quotes the last line of the announcer's words from the ברייתא in step 19.

phrases.english: and a creditor his debt"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why one specific detail of the announcement listed in step 19 is needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What a buyer gains from hearing that the money goes to a wife's כתובה or a creditor's debt.

steps.title: Different buyers prefer different payees
steps.stepSummary: Some buyers prefer paying a creditor, who is easygoing about the coins. Others prefer paying a woman, who accepts payment bit by bit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because some buyers prefer dealing with a creditor, since he is easygoing about the coins. And some prefer dealing with a woman, since she takes the money little by little.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that who receives the money does matter to buyers. Each type of payee offers the buyer a different advantage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creditor is flexible about the coins he accepts. A woman collecting her כתובה lets the buyer pay in small amounts over time. Announcing who gets paid draws in buyers who like that kind of arrangement, which helps the field sell well.

keyTerms.meaning: He prefers it, it is convenient for him
He is easygoing about the coins he accepts
Coins, money
Little by little, in small payments

steps.whatToRemember: The announcement says who gets the money so that every type of buyer is drawn in. Some like a flexible creditor, and some like a woman who takes small payments.

phrases.english: Because there is someone who prefers dealing with a creditor
since he is easygoing about the coins
phrases.notes: The creditor doesn't fuss over the exact quality of the coins he is given.

phrases.english: and there is someone who prefers dealing with a woman
since she takes payment little by little

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Naming the payee draws buyers who prefer that payee's terms. A creditor is flexible about coins, and a woman accepts payment in installments.
